reader.title: Expulsion of Williams, a Black constable-elect near Atlanta
bases: A vigilance committee warned an elected Black constable to leave or be hanged and he left; no violence beyond the threat is reported (A2).
No one was killed: Williams received a threat of hanging from a 'vigilance committee', whose size is not given, and left (A2). The stated pretext was racial, that no 'niggers' could hold office (A2).
The only report is a Canton, Ohio, dispatch relaying Williams's own account, with no confirmation from Georgia (A2).

summary.text: The expulsion of Williams was the forced departure, in November 1888, of a Black man who said he had been elected constable in a country district about twenty miles from Atlanta, Georgia, and was ordered by a "vigilance committee" to leave or be hanged.
He left the state and told his story a month later in Canton, Ohio, where a brief dispatch carried it to the Northern press under the headline "Driven Away Because He Was Elected."
According to his own account, Williams was elected constable in the district on November 6, 1888.
The next day, he said, a vigilance committee warned him that no "niggers" could hold office and that he must leave or be hanged.
He left, and said he worked his way North, spending several days in and around Canton by early December.
The dispatch gave only his surname and did not name the district, the county or any member of the committee.
No report of an arrest, investigation or official response in Georgia appears in the coverage, and no confirmation of the election from a Georgia source was found.
The story survives in a Canton, Ohio, dispatch dated December 5 and printed the next day by the Indianapolis Journal among a column of short telegraphic items.
The dispatch called it "a strange story," described Williams as "intelligent," and quoted the committee's slur in quotation marks, but offered no comment on the committee and no check of his claims.
Because the Black-press collection begins in 1900, no Black newspaper's version is available, and no other white paper's reprint was found.

accounts.label: Williams's own account (Canton dispatch)
accounts.gist: Elected constable Nov. 6 in a district twenty miles from Atlanta, he was warned the next day by a vigilance committee that no "niggers" could hold office and that he must leave or be hanged; he left.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Driven Away Because He Was Elected' in a column of brief wire items; it called his tale 'a strange story' and the man 'intelligent', without comment on the committee.

record_check.dossier: Intimidation/forced departure of one man; no killing or attempt is reported, only a threat of hanging.
No crime alleged; the pretext was that a Black man could not hold office.
An organized 'vigilance committee' rather than a crowd.
Unnamed country district twenty miles from Atlanta; county not given.

info: Williams said he was elected constable on Nov. 6, 1888, and received the warning the next day (Nov. 7).
A country district twenty miles from Atlanta, Ga.; the district and county are not named.
A colored man who gave his name as Williams; no first name given.
No crime alleged; the warning said no "niggers" could hold office.
Williams left Georgia and was in and around Canton, Ohio, by early December 1888.

sources.note: Canton, O., Dec. 5 dispatch, 'Driven Away Because He Was Elected': Williams's own account of being elected constable near Atlanta on Nov. 6 and warned next day by a vigilance committee to leave or be hanged.

The man, who is intelligent, says he worked his way North, and gives his name as Williams.
